As shown in the figure, an object with a mass of $2\mathrm{kg}$ is placed on a horizontal ground. Under the action of a force of magnitude $20\mathrm{N}$ directed at an angle of $37^{\circ}$ above the horizontal, the object starts from rest and moves a distance of $10\mathrm{m}$ in 2 seconds. The gravitational acceleration is taken as $g=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$, $\sin37^{\circ}{=}0.6$, and $\cos37^{\circ}{=}0.8$.

1. The magnitude of the velocity of the object at the end of 3 seconds.
2. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the object and the horizontal surface.
3. If the pulling force is removed at the end of 3 seconds, how much farther can the object move?

Therefore the pulling force has a horizontal component to the right, and also has an upward vertical component, which will reduce the supporting force of the ground on the object. Reasoning: The object starts from rest, and under the action of the pulling force moves 10 m within 2 s. According to uniformly accelerated linear motion, s = (1/2)at^2, so 10 = (1/2)a(2^2), giving a = 5 m/s^2. The pulling force continues to act until the end of 3 s, therefore the velocity at the end of 3 s is v = at = 5 × 3 = 15 m/s. Decomposition of the pulling force: F_x = F cos37° = 20 × 0.8 = 16 N, F_y = F sin37° = 20 × 0.6 = 12 N. There is no acceleration in the vertical direction, so N = mg - F_y = 2 × 10 - 12 = 8 N. In the horizontal direction, by Newton's second law: F_x - μN = ma, that is 16 - 8μ = 2 × 5 = 10, solving gives μ = 0.75. After the pulling force is removed at the end of 3 s, the upward component of the pulling force disappears, and the supporting force becomes N' = mg. At this time the kinetic friction force f = μmg, and the magnitude of the deceleration a' = f/m = μg = 0.75 × 10 = 7.5 m/s^2. The velocity at the instant the force is removed is 15 m/s, and the stopping distance x = v^2/(2a') = 15^2/(2 × 7.5) = 15 m.

method.method_draft: Describe the image first: a block rests on a horizontal surface and is pulled by a force F directed up and to the right at 37° above the horizontal, so the force has a rightward horizontal component and an upward vertical component that reduces the normal force. Use constant-acceleration kinematics: s=(1/2)at^2 gives a=5 m/s^2, so v at 3 s is at=15 m/s. Then apply Newton's second law vertically and horizontally while the force acts: N=mg-Fsin37°=20-12=8 N, and Fcos37°-μN=ma, so 16-8μ=10, giving μ=0.75. After the force is removed, the image-grounded upward pulling component disappears; the normal becomes mg and kinetic friction is μmg. The deceleration is μg=7.5 m/s^2, so the stopping distance from 15 m/s is v^2/(2μg)=15 m.

ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot:
Image description: In the figure there is a block placed on a horizontal ground indicated by diagonal-line shading; from the upper right of the block acts a pulling force F directed obliquely upward to the right, and the angle between the pulling force and the horizontal dashed-line direction is marked as 37°. Therefore the pulling force has a horizontal component to the right, and also has an upward vertical component, which will reduce the supporting force of the ground on the object.

Reasoning: The object starts from rest, and under the action of the pulling force moves 10 m within 2 s. According to uniformly accelerated linear motion, s = (1/2)at^2, so 10 = (1/2)a(2^2), giving a = 5 m/s^2. The pulling force continues to act until the end of 3 s, therefore the velocity at the end of 3 s is v = at = 5 × 3 = 15 m/s.

Decomposition of the pulling force: F_x = F cos37° = 20 × 0.8 = 16 N, F_y = F sin37° = 20 × 0.6 = 12 N. There is no acceleration in the vertical direction, so N = mg - F_y = 2 × 10 - 12 = 8 N. In the horizontal direction, by Newton's second law: F_x - μN = ma, that is 16 - 8μ = 2 × 5 = 10, solving gives μ = 0.75.

After the pulling force is removed at the end of 3 s, the upward component of the pulling force disappears, and the supporting force becomes N' = mg. At this time the kinetic friction force f = μmg, and the magnitude of the deceleration a' = f/m = μg = 0.75 × 10 = 7.5 m/s^2. The velocity at the instant the force is removed is 15 m/s, and the stopping distance x = v^2/(2a') = 15^2/(2 × 7.5) = 15 m.
